newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jerusalem tunnel the spark for frustrated Arabs.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem tunnel the spark for frustrated Arabs.

text.p: Palestinians are venting months of frustration over slow-moving peace talks in clashes with Israelis, but the spark was an Israeli-dug tunnel near a holy Moslem shrine.

The violence, which has killed 44 Palestinians and 11 Israelis since Wednesday, is a bloody reminder that Jerusalem's holy sites remain at the heart of the explosive struggle between Moslem and Jew in the Holy Land.
The 488-metre (yard) tunnel is adjacent to the Temple Mount, once home to ancient Jewish Temples and now the site of the al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third holiest shrine.

It snakes beneath the walled Old City along an ancient water tunnel and excavated parts of the Wailing Wall, the sole remnant of the Temple complex and a retaining wall for the mosque compound known as Haram al-Sharif, Arabic for "the holy sanctuary".

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat called the opening of the tunnel a "crime" and an attempt to "Judaise" the city. Moslem officials at al-Aqsa charge Israel with trying to undermine the integrity of Islamic holy sites.

"The digging has caused some Islamic Waqf (Trust) buildings near al-Aqsa to crack and we had to renovate them. We are worried that this would lead to the collapse of these holy sites," Jerusalem Mufti Sheikh Ikrima Sabri told Reuters.

Jerusalem's Israeli Mayor Ehud Olmert rejected the charge, telling reporters: "All this rhetoric and misinformation about the danger to the infrastructure of the Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem is sheer nonsense."
"The tunnel is so far away from all the Moslem holy sites in the Temple Mount," Olmert said.

The tunnel, a window to the ancient history of Jerusalem and a point of reverence for religious Jews, has been open for some time with only one entry and exit point in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City.
Israel this week made a new opening to the tunnel on the Via Dolorosa in the Old City's Moslem Quarter, sparking widespread violence that threatens to crush what is left of the peace process.

"We didn't harm the freedom of religion. We didn't harm anyone here in his ability to pray anywhere. We simply opened an entrance to an existing tunnel," Israeli Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani told reporters in the tunnel.
Israel hopes the second entrance will increase the number of tourists who visit the site from 70,000 to 400,000 a year.
Waqf officials said the digging near al-Aqsa mosque was done without the knowledge or approval of the Islamic Trust, on Moslem property.
"The digging of the tunnel was done on Islamic Waqf property and is a violation of the holiness of Moslem and Christian rights," Sabri told Reuters.
"The new entrance leads to the Mujahideen path used by Moslems to reach al-Aqsa and used by Christians to go to their churches."

The struggle between Moslem and Jew has exploded several times on the Temple Mount. In October 1990 Israeli police shot dead 17 Palestinians during a clash when thousands of Arabs stoned thousands of Jews praying at the Wailing Wall.
During a Jewish festival in 1986 a grenade attack by Islamic fundamentalists killed one Israeli and wounded 69 at an army ceremony below the Temple Mount.
On Easter Sunday in 1982 a Jewish-American gunman shot up the Temple Mount, killing one person in a rampage that ignited weeks of Palestinian unrest in which four Arabs were killed.
In September 1969 a mentally disturbed visitor from Australia entered al-Aqsa mosque and started a fire.
